Pregnancy

Metformin before and during pregnancy: benefits, uncertainties and breastfeeding

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Metformin can be appropriate in pregnancy, but the reason you take it matters. Treatment for type 2 diabetes, treatment for gestational diabetes and treatment to help ovulation are different decisions. A positive pregnancy test is a reason to review your prescription promptly with your team, not to stop essential glucose treatment or assume that every prescription should continue unchanged.

What metformin does

Metformin is a prescription medicine that lowers blood glucose, partly by reducing glucose production in the liver and helping the body respond to insulin. Insulin resistance means insulin is less effective at helping the body use glucose. Metformin does not replace insulin when insulin is needed, and it is not a treatment for an acute diabetic emergency.

It is also used for selected metabolic and fertility problems in polycystic ovary syndrome, traditionally called PCOS. In 2026 this condition was renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS; older studies and records still use PCOS. It can affect ovulation and metabolic health. Having it does not mean that every ovarian cyst needs metformin or that everyone has the same degree of insulin resistance.

Before conception, review the whole treatment plan

If you have diabetes, ask for a preconception appointment to review glucose control, medicines, kidney and eye health, nutrition and folic acid. Good control before conception and throughout pregnancy reduces risks, including miscarriage and congenital abnormalities, but cannot eliminate every risk. The aim is a sustainable plan that also avoids dangerous low glucose.

Bring the actual packaging and a list of all medicines and supplements. A tablet containing metformin plus another drug needs a separate check: reassurance about metformin does not automatically apply to its other ingredient. Discuss pregnancy plans before changing contraception, and tell the team promptly about an unexpected pregnancy. Ask for a plan you can understand and follow, including help with costs or supplies.

Can it help someone with PCOS become pregnant?

Metformin can improve ovulation and pregnancy chances in some people with PCOS/PMOS, but it is not the most effective ovulation medicine for everyone. The international guideline recommends letrozole first for infertility due to absent ovulation when there are no other infertility factors. Metformin may have a selected role alone or alongside other treatment, especially when metabolic needs also matter.

Assessment should consider age, ovulation and other possible fertility factors rather than treating a scan description alone. Improved cycles do not guarantee conception or a live birth, and metformin is not contraception. Ovulation-induction treatment and treatment after conception have different purposes; agree in advance whom to call after a positive test and whether the medicine's original indication still applies.

What changes after a positive pregnancy test?

Contact the prescriber or maternity/diabetes team promptly. They need to know whether metformin was prescribed for diabetes, metabolic concerns or ovulation, your gestational stage, current glucose results and any other medicines. Continuing, changing or stopping it should be an explicit clinical decision with a monitoring plan. Do not stop prescribed insulin or leave diabetes untreated while waiting for a routine visit.

For metformin used specifically for PCOS-related ovulation induction, ADA 2026 guidance recommends discontinuation by the end of the first trimester. The international PCOS guideline does not recommend routine use throughout pregnancy, although selected circumstances may justify it. These statements are not an instruction to choose your own stop date: diabetes or another continuing indication may change the plan, and abrupt loss of glucose control can be harmful.

Type 2 diabetes: metformin, insulin or both

In US ADA guidance, insulin is preferred for type 2 diabetes in pregnancy. UK guidance and product information permit metformin in selected pregnancies when clinically needed, including as an addition or alternative to insulin. Differences reflect how benefits, placental exposure, uncertainties, glucose response and practical access are weighed. Ask which recommendation your team is following and why it fits your circumstances.

Adding metformin is not a guarantee of a healthier newborn. Large trials of metformin added to insulin did not improve the overall combined neonatal outcome; some outcomes, including infant size and maternal insulin needs, differed. A 2026 secondary analysis suggested benefits in some subgroups but needs confirmation. Concerns about small fetal size, placental function, hypertension or pre-eclampsia require particular specialist consideration, not self-selection from a trial result.

Gestational diabetes is a separate indication

Gestational diabetes develops during pregnancy and usually begins with individual nutrition advice, suitable activity and glucose monitoring. If medication is needed, ADA prefers insulin. NICE offers metformin in selected cases when targets remain unmet after diet and activity changes, adding insulin if necessary; some people need insulin promptly from diagnosis. There is no worldwide rule that one medicine must always come first.

Needing insulin alongside metformin does not mean you have failed. Your team sets targets and reviews the pattern of readings, not just one reassuring number. Metformin alone may be insufficient. Ask when to report out-of-range results and what to do during illness; do not increase tablets, borrow insulin or use herbal glucose remedies to correct readings on your own.

It is not a general prevention or weight-loss medicine in pregnancy

For pregnant people with PCOS/PMOS, the international guideline has not shown metformin to prevent gestational diabetes, late miscarriage, hypertension, pre-eclampsia or a very large baby. Evidence does not justify promising that it prevents miscarriage generally. Selected use to reduce preterm birth or limit excessive gestational weight gain may be considered, but this is different from routine prevention for everyone at risk.

Taking it during pregnancy is also not a general guarantee against future type 2 diabetes. After pregnancy, some people with prediabetes and previous gestational diabetes may benefit from metformin and lifestyle support to reduce progression risk; that is a separate assessment. Do not use metformin or restrictive dieting to try to lose weight during pregnancy. Discuss nutrition and an appropriate weight-gain plan without blame.

What is known about the fetus and later childhood?

Metformin crosses the placenta. Available human evidence is reassuring about major congenital abnormalities after early exposure, and metformin is not expected to increase miscarriage risk. This does not mean every pregnancy is risk-free or that the medicine has no possible effects. Poorly controlled diabetes itself can cause harm, so safety discussions must compare realistic treatment options with the risks of inadequate treatment.

Studies of birth size and later child growth have produced mixed results. Some follow-up studies suggest greater childhood weight; others do not, and causality and longer-term effects remain uncertain. Exposure alone does not usually require ending a pregnancy or extra fetal tests beyond those indicated by diabetes and other risks. Your team should explain the reason for growth scans and newborn glucose checks rather than promise that a normal scan answers every safety question.

Side effects and checks worth discussing

Nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort and reduced appetite are common, particularly when treatment starts. Taking the prescribed preparation with food or a clinician-led change in formulation or dose can help. Do not assume severe pain, persistent vomiting or inability to drink is an ordinary side effect. Report troublesome symptoms and ask what to do before taking the next dose if you are becoming dehydrated.

Kidney function needs assessment because metformin can accumulate when clearance falls. The team should also know about liver disease, severe infection, heart or breathing illness and other medicines. Long-term metformin can lower vitamin B12: new marked tiredness, a sore red tongue, tingling or anaemia deserves assessment. Testing is guided by symptoms and risk factors; B12 deficiency can often be treated without stopping otherwise appropriate metformin.

Illness and low glucose need a written plan

Ask for specific sick-day instructions before you need them. Dehydration from severe vomiting or diarrhoea, fever or reduced fluid intake can make metformin unsafe; its product information advises temporary withholding and prompt professional contact in dehydration. Obtain urgent advice about the next dose, glucose monitoring and safe restart. Follow an existing clinician-issued plan, and do not apply a metformin pause to insulin: insulin must not simply be stopped because you are not eating.

Metformin alone rarely causes low glucose, but insulin or certain other diabetes medicines can. Learn your own low-glucose signs and treatment plan, keep fast-acting carbohydrate available and recheck as instructed. Repeated lows, high readings not responding to the agreed treatment, or difficulty keeping food and fluids down need prompt team advice. If you cannot swallow safely or become unconscious, nothing should be given by mouth; someone should summon emergency help and use prescribed glucagon only if trained.

Symptoms that need emergency help

Seek emergency care if lactic acidosis is suspected while taking metformin: for example, unusual severe weakness with breathing difficulty, abdominal pain, vomiting or muscle cramps. Stop metformin and get help rather than taking another dose to correct glucose. Suspected diabetic ketoacidosis, with symptoms such as deep breathing, fruity breath, vomiting, drowsiness or confusion, also needs emergency assessment; do not wait for a very high glucose result or for every sign to appear. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance.

Call emergency services for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat; struggling or very rapid breathing; throat tightness or difficulty swallowing; blue, grey or pale skin, lips or tongue; sudden marked confusion, sudden drowsiness or sudden dizziness; or fainting with inability to wake. These are independent possible anaphylaxis signs, and a rash is not required. Use your prescribed adrenaline auto-injector if available and call for an ambulance. In pregnancy lie on your left side; if breathing is difficult, raise your shoulders carefully. Do not stand or walk.

Taking it safely in everyday life

Use the exact product and schedule prescribed for you. Immediate-release, modified-release, liquid and combination preparations are not interchangeable instructions. Do not double a dose to make up for one missed; check your leaflet or pharmacist's advice. Taking more than prescribed needs urgent medical advice even if you initially feel well. Keep packaging available when seeking help.

Before surgery, an anaesthetic or an investigation using iodinated contrast, tell the team that you take metformin and are pregnant. They may need a temporary interruption and a kidney-function-based restart plan. Tell the pharmacist about painkillers, diuretics, blood-pressure medicines, vitamins and herbal products too. An online list cannot replace checking your actual combination, and metformin does not make alcohol safe in pregnancy.

Birth and the weeks afterwards

Agree the medicine and glucose plan for labour, birth and discharge before the due date when possible. Insulin needs can fall quickly after birth. For gestational diabetes, glucose-lowering treatment is commonly stopped after delivery under the maternity team's plan, followed by testing to check whether diabetes persists. Pre-existing type 2 diabetes still needs treatment and a clear handover.

A baby may need early feeding support and glucose checks because of the pregnancy's diabetes and treatment context. Ask what monitoring is planned. Book the recommended postnatal glucose test even if you feel well, then ongoing screening and future-pregnancy advice. Do not assume a normal home reading proves diabetes has gone, or continue an old pregnancy dose automatically once you are home.

Can you breastfeed while taking metformin?

Metformin enters milk in very small amounts. NHS specialist breastfeeding guidance considers it a preferred option for diabetes when the infant is full term and healthy, with monitoring. Advice needs individual review for a premature or unwell infant, a newborn with particular concerns, kidney problems, or several maternal medicines. Small milk exposure is reassuring but is not a guarantee about every infant's growth or health.

Some product leaflets are more cautious because data are limited; a clinician or breastfeeding medicines specialist can reconcile the leaflet with current specialist guidance and your baby's situation. Do not stop feeding or needed treatment solely because the wording differs. Ask about vomiting, diarrhoea, unusual sleepiness, pallor, sweating or shakiness and weight gain. An unwell baby needs prompt assessment, rather than assuming the symptoms are caused by milk or metformin.

Make the next decision with your team

A useful review answers four questions: why am I taking metformin now, what benefit is expected for this indication, what alternatives or uncertainties matter, and when will the plan be reassessed? Include pregnancy stage, kidney health, glucose patterns, tolerability and feeding plans. Ask who can help urgently outside normal clinic hours and what changes require contact.

Keep a short record of prescribed medicines, glucose results if requested, symptoms and questions. BeMama can help organise this information, but it cannot decide whether to continue metformin, interpret fetal growth or calculate a dose. A written shared plan should guide care through conception, pregnancy and breastfeeding; a reassuring general article cannot replace your individual review.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the prescriber to record the current indication, pregnancy plan, monitoring and circumstances for a treatment change.

Get written illness, missed-dose, emergency-contact, postpartum and breastfeeding instructions for your actual medicines and infant.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can organise your prescribed medicine list, clinician-set glucose targets, symptoms and appointment questions. It cannot prescribe metformin or insulin, diagnose lactic acidosis, assess fetal growth or determine infant medicine safety. Contact clinical services directly for urgent concerns.

When to seek help

Do not stop needed insulin or make routine metformin changes yourself. Dehydration needs prompt advice and the agreed temporary-withholding plan. Suspected lactic acidosis while taking metformin requires stopping it and emergency care; suspected ketoacidosis also needs emergency assessment. Sudden mouth/throat swelling, breathing/swallowing difficulty, blue/grey/pale colour, sudden marked confusion, sudden drowsiness or sudden dizziness or unresponsive fainting are independent possible anaphylaxis emergencies, even without a rash. Use prescribed adrenaline and call an ambulance. Do not drive yourself; give nothing by mouth to someone unable to swallow safely.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Metformin can be appropriate in pregnancy; the indication and individual circumstances determine the plan.
  • Fertility use for PCOS/PMOS is different from treatment of established diabetes after conception.
  • UK and US guidelines differ on medicine choice; do not stop insulin or change treatment yourself.
  • Early fetal safety evidence is reassuring, while birth-size and longer-term child outcomes still have uncertainties.
  • Illness, kidney health, B12, postpartum doses and breastfeeding all deserve a specific follow-up plan.

Frequently asked questions

What does metformin do?

It lowers glucose partly by reducing liver glucose production and improving insulin action. It is prescribed for type 2 or gestational diabetes and selected PCOS/PMOS needs. It does not replace insulin when insulin is needed or treat an acute diabetic emergency.

Does it treat ovarian cysts or guarantee pregnancy?

No. Selected people with PCOS/PMOS may ovulate more regularly, but not every cyst represents this condition and conception is not guaranteed. Letrozole is the guideline's first ovulation medicine for anovulatory infertility without other factors; the best plan follows assessment.

Should I stop when my pregnancy test is positive?

Contact the prescriber promptly for an indication-specific plan. ADA recommends stopping ovulation-only PCOS use by the end of the first trimester, but ongoing diabetes can change that decision. Do not choose a stop date yourself or stop prescribed insulin.

Can it prevent miscarriage or gestational diabetes?

It should not be promised for either purpose. In pregnant people with PCOS/PMOS it has not been shown to prevent gestational diabetes or late miscarriage. Selected preterm-birth or excessive-weight-gain considerations are different from universal prevention.

Will it harm the baby?

Evidence about major birth defects after early exposure is reassuring, but no treatment or pregnancy is risk-free. Metformin crosses the placenta; birth-size and long-term child-growth findings are mixed. Compare those uncertainties with the risks of poorly controlled diabetes and the available alternatives.

Why might I need insulin too?

Metformin may not achieve pregnancy glucose targets alone. ADA prefers insulin for type 2 and gestational diabetes, while UK care includes selected metformin use. Adding or changing treatment is based on your readings and risks, not a judgement about effort.

Can I breastfeed?

Often yes after an individual medicine check, especially with a healthy full-term infant. Milk levels are small, but premature, unwell or kidney-affected infants need specialist advice. Discuss cautious leaflet wording, infant symptoms and weight gain rather than automatically stopping treatment or breastfeeding.

When should I get urgent help?

Dehydration, inability to keep fluids down, repeated lows or uncontrolled high readings need prompt clinical advice. Suspected lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis needs emergency care. Sudden mouth or throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty, blue/grey/pale colour, sudden marked confusion, sudden drowsiness or sudden dizziness or unresponsive fainting can signal anaphylaxis; call emergency services without waiting for a rash or all signs. Do not drive yourself or give anything by mouth to someone unable to swallow safely.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
